classification.reason: 'At', 'on', and 'in' connect an action or event to a time. They answer the question 'When?'

similarities: All three usually come before a time word or time phrase.
All three can answer the question 'When does it happen?'
differences: Use 'at' for a very exact time: at 8:30, at noon, at midnight.
Use 'on' for one specific day or date: on Monday, on July 1st, on my birthday.
Use 'in' for a bigger time period: in April, in 2026, in summer, in the morning.
Choose 'at' when the time feels like a point.
Choose 'on' when the time is a day or date on a calendar.
Choose 'in' when the time is inside a longer period.

association.note: These prepositions often appear with time words students already know: clock times, days, dates, months, seasons, and years.

counterExample.reason: This is wrong because '8:00' is an exact clock time. The correct sentence is: 'I go to school at 8:00.'

counterExample.wrong: We have English class in Monday.
counterExample.reason: This is wrong because 'Monday' is a day of the week. The correct sentence is: 'We have English class on Monday.'
This is wrong because 'August' is a month, not a full date. The correct sentence is: 'My vacation starts in August.'

scenario.description: Office: The meeting is at 10:00 on Friday in March. School: Math class starts at 9:15 on Tuesday. Travel: We arrive at night on July 3rd. Daily conversation: I play games in the evening. Academic writing: The study began in 2024. Business email: The call is on Monday at 2 p.m.

mnemonic.content: Think: AT = a small point on a clock, ON = one square on a calendar, IN = inside a big box of time.

confusion.confusedWith: in the morning vs on Monday morning
confusion.reason: Use 'in the morning' for a general part of the day. Use 'on Monday morning' when the morning belongs to a specific day.

conversation.speaker: Mina
conversation.text: Let us study in the evening.
